title: Siege of Leningrad lifted
place: Leningrad (St Petersburg) and its southern approaches
casualties: Soviet c. 310,000 killed, wounded or sick in the Leningrad–Novgorod offensive (Jan–Mar 1944); German losses heavy but less certain; over the whole siege c. 800,000 or more civilians of Leningrad died
summary: Soviet attacks from the Oranienbaum pocket and the Pulkovo Heights break the German ring around Leningrad. On 27 January the city's guns fire a salute: after some 872 days, the siege is over.
detail:
In January 1944 the Leningrad and Volkhov Fronts struck the German Eighteenth Army, which had held its siege lines since September 1941. On 14 January Fedyuninsky's 2nd Shock Army attacked out of the coastal bridgehead at Oranienbaum; the next day Maslennikov's 42nd Army went forward from the Pulkovo Heights, south of the city. After a week of fighting through fortified villages the two forces met near Ropsha, trapping and destroying the German heavy artillery that had shelled Leningrad for more than two years. To the south-east, Meretskov's Volkhov Front retook a ruined Novgorod on 20 January.

On 27 January, with the railway to Moscow cleared, Govorov declared the city fully freed and Leningrad celebrated with a salute from hundreds of guns. Küchler, who had pleaded to retreat, was dismissed; Model pulled Army Group North back to the Panther Line by the end of February.

The siege had been one of the gravest crimes of the war: the German command had chosen to starve the city rather than take it, and in the winter of 1941–42 alone hundreds of thousands of civilians died of hunger and cold.
significance: The end of the blockade freed the Soviet Union's second city and a whole front for the offensives of 1944, and closed the most lethal siege of modern history.
uncertaintyNote: The number of civilian dead in the siege is disputed: Soviet-era figures of c. 632,000 are now regarded as too low, and estimates run from c. 800,000 to over 1 million. The phrase 'about 900 days' is traditional; 8 September 1941 to 27 January 1944 is 872 days.
sources: David M. Glantz, The Battle for Leningrad 1941–1944 (2002)
Anna Reid, Leningrad: Tragedy of a City under Siege, 1941–44 (2011)
David M. Glantz and Jonathan M. House, When Titans Clashed (1995)

title: Battles of Monte Cassino
place: Cassino and Monte Cassino, on the Gustav Line, Lazio, Italy

sides.opponent: Britain and the Commonwealth, United States, France, Poland

casualties: Allied c. 55,000; German c. 20,000 (four battles, figures approximate)
summary: Four Allied assaults over four months batter the Gustav Line where it bars the road to Rome. The ancient abbey is bombed to rubble; Polish troops finally raise their flag over its ruins.
detail:
The Gustav Line ran across Italy at its narrowest, and at Cassino it blocked the Liri valley, the natural road to Rome. The first battle began on 17 January 1944: British troops crossed the Garigliano, but the US 36th Division was cut to pieces trying to cross the Rapido on 20–22 January.

In February, convinced that the Germans were using the Benedictine abbey on the summit, the Allies destroyed it on 15 February with more than 200 bombers; German paratroops then fortified the ruins. New Zealand and Indian attacks failed, and in March a second bombing flattened Cassino town, whose rubble proved ideal ground for its defenders.

The fourth battle, Operation Diadem, opened on 11 May with a massive attack along the whole front. Juin's French Expeditionary Corps, many of them Moroccan and Algerian troops, broke through the Aurunci Mountains, and on 18 May the Polish II Corps, after terrible losses, took the abbey ruins. In the villages behind the line, soldiers of the corps committed mass rapes of Italian civilians, a crime long remembered in the region.
significance: Cassino opened the way to Rome, but at a price that made it the Western Allies' most costly battle in Italy and a byword for attritional fighting.
uncertaintyNote: Whether German troops used the abbey before the bombing is still argued; most evidence suggests they did not occupy the building itself. Casualty totals vary with how the four battles are bounded.
sources: Matthew Parker, Monte Cassino (2003)
John Ellis, Cassino: The Hollow Victory (1984)
Rick Atkinson, The Day of Battle (2007)

title: Landing at Anzio
place: Anzio and Nettuno, on the coast south of Rome
casualties: Allied c. 43,000 (c. 7,000 killed); German c. 40,000 (c. 5,000 killed); figures approximate
summary: An Allied corps lands almost unopposed behind the Gustav Line, but stays in its beachhead. Kesselring rings it with troops, and a four-month siege follows before the breakout in May.
detail:
Operation Shingle was meant to unhinge the Gustav Line by landing behind it, 50 km from Rome. On 22 January 1944 Lucas's VI Corps, American and British, came ashore at Anzio and Nettuno against almost no resistance. Lucas, with few troops and scarred by Salerno, chose to consolidate rather than strike inland for the Alban Hills.

Kesselring reacted with speed, rushing units from northern Italy, France and the Balkans. A US Ranger force was all but destroyed at Cisterna on 30 January, and on 16 February Mackensen's Fourteenth Army counter-attacked down the Albano road and nearly reached the sea before Allied artillery and naval gunfire stopped it. Churchill complained that instead of a wildcat hurled ashore he had got a stranded whale. Truscott replaced Lucas, and the beachhead, every part of it within range of German guns, settled into trench warfare.

On 23 May, as Diadem broke the Gustav Line, VI Corps broke out, and on 25 May it joined hands with the main Fifth Army advancing from the south.
significance: Anzio failed in its aim of a quick road to Rome, but it tied down German divisions and its breakout helped turn Diadem into the fall of Rome.
uncertaintyNote: Casualty totals vary between sources depending on whether sickness is included.
sources: Carlo D'Este, Fatal Decision: Anzio and the Battle for Rome (1991)
Rick Atkinson, The Day of Battle (2007)
Lloyd Clark, Anzio: The Friction of War (2006)

title: Korsun–Cherkassy pocket
place: Around Korsun and Shenderovka, west of Cherkassy, Ukraine

strength.focus: XI and XLII Corps, c. 56,000–60,000 men encircled, with relief attacks by III and XLVII Panzer Corps

casualties: German c. 20,000 lost in the pocket, including Stemmermann; c. 40,000 broke out, leaving their heavy weapons. Soviet losses c. 80,000 killed and wounded across the operation
summary: Two Soviet fronts encircle two German corps on the Dnieper bend; after three weeks most of the trapped troops break out on foot, but the corps are destroyed as fighting units.
detail:
Hitler insisted on holding a salient on the Dnieper south of Kiev, the last stretch of the river in German hands. On 24 and 26 January 1944 Konev's 2nd and Vatutin's 1st Ukrainian Fronts attacked its shoulders and met at Zvenigorodka on 28 January, trapping XI and XLII Corps, including the SS Wiking Division and the Belgian Walloon Brigade. Manstein sent panzer corps to cut through, but thaw and mud bogged them down short of the pocket at Lysianka.

On the night of 16–17 February, in a snowstorm, the trapped troops broke out towards the relief force. Columns were cut up by tanks and artillery on the open slopes near Shenderovka and Pochapintsy, and thousands drowned or froze crossing the icy Gniloy Tikich stream. Stemmermann was killed. Some 40,000 men reached German lines, but almost all their guns and vehicles were lost.
significance: Korsun destroyed six German divisions as fighting formations and opened the way for the Soviet spring offensives that cleared most of western Ukraine.
uncertaintyNote: Soviet claims of 55,000 Germans killed and 18,000 captured are much too high; the German figures here follow Zetterling and Frankson. Soviet losses are estimates.
sources: Niklas Zetterling and Anders Frankson, The Korsun Pocket: The Encirclement and Breakout of a German Army in the East, 1944 (2008)
Douglas E. Nash, Hell's Gate: The Battle of the Cherkassy Pocket (2002)
David M. Glantz and Jonathan House, When Titans Clashed (rev. ed. 2015)

title: Kwajalein and the Marshall Islands
place: Kwajalein Atoll, Marshall Islands

strength.focus: c. 8,000 men, many of them naval personnel and labourers
strength.opponent: 4th Marine Division and 7th Infantry Division, c. 42,000 men

casualties: Japanese c. 7,900 dead, a few hundred taken prisoner (many of them Korean labourers); US c. 370 killed and 1,600 wounded
summary: US Marines and soldiers seize Kwajalein, at the heart of Japan's Marshall Islands, in four days, at a fraction of the cost of Tarawa.
detail:
Having learned hard lessons at Tarawa, Nimitz bypassed the outer Marshalls and struck straight at Kwajalein, the world's largest atoll and the Japanese headquarters in the group. Operation Flintlock opened with days of bombardment from battleships and carrier aircraft, far heavier than at Tarawa. On 31 January 1944 troops seized small islets to site artillery, and the next day the 4th Marine Division landed on Roi-Namur in the north while the 7th Infantry Division landed on Kwajalein Island in the south. Amphibious tractors and better naval gunfire support carried the troops ashore.

Roi-Namur fell in two days, despite a blockhouse full of torpedo warheads that blew up and killed twenty Marines; Kwajalein Island was cleared by 4 February. The garrisons fought almost to the last man. Majuro had already been taken unopposed, and Spruance moved quickly on to Eniwetok, taken between 17 and 23 February.
significance: The swift capture of the Marshalls showed that the US Navy could leap across the central Pacific, advanced its timetable by months, and gave the fleet the anchorages from which it struck Truk and the Marianas.
uncertaintyNote: US totals combine figures for Roi-Namur and Kwajalein Island; Japanese dead are estimates from the burial count.
sources: Philip A. Crowl and Edmund G. Love, Seizure of the Gilberts and Marshalls (US Army official history, 1955)
Ian W. Toll, The Conquering Tide: War in the Pacific Islands, 1942–1944 (2015)
Samuel Eliot Morison, History of United States Naval Operations in World War II, vol. VII (1951)

title: Operation Hailstone: the raid on Truk
place: Truk Lagoon (Chuuk), Caroline Islands

strength.focus: c. 350 aircraft and the ships remaining in the lagoon
strength.opponent: Task Force 58: 5 fleet and 4 light carriers, 6 battleships, with cruisers and destroyers

casualties: Japanese: c. 250 aircraft destroyed, 12 warships and over 30 merchant ships (c. 200,000 tons) sunk, several thousand killed; US: 25 aircraft lost, c. 40 killed, the carrier Intrepid torpedoed
summary: American carrier aircraft strike Japan's great fleet base at Truk for two days, sinking dozens of ships and destroying most of its aircraft.
detail:
Truk, with its huge lagoon, had been the Combined Fleet's forward base since 1942 and was thought by the Allies to be a Pacific Gibraltar. Warned by American reconnaissance flights, Admiral Koga withdrew the battleships and carriers to Palau and Japan a week before the blow fell. But on 17 February 1944 Mitscher's carriers struck at dawn, sweeping the Japanese fighters from the sky and then attacking the airfields and the shipping crowded in the lagoon.

Over two days the strikes sank cruisers, destroyers, auxiliaries and a large fleet of transports and tankers; Spruance took battleships round the atoll to sink ships fleeing through the passes, including the light cruiser Katori. A night torpedo attack damaged the carrier Intrepid. The ships of the merchant fleet still lie on the floor of the lagoon.
significance: Hailstone ended Truk's usefulness as a fleet base, letting the Americans bypass it altogether, and the loss of so many tankers and transports deepened Japan's shipping crisis.
uncertaintyNote: Counts of ships and aircraft destroyed vary between accounts, depending on how small craft and damaged aircraft are counted.
sources: Ian W. Toll, The Conquering Tide: War in the Pacific Islands, 1942–1944 (2015)
Samuel Eliot Morison, History of United States Naval Operations in World War II, vol. VII (1951)
Klaus Lindemann, Hailstorm over Truk Lagoon (1982)

title: Imphal and Kohima
place: Imphal plain and Kohima ridge, Manipur and the Naga Hills, India
casualties: Japanese c. 55,000–60,000 (perhaps half dead, many from starvation and disease); British and Indian c. 17,000
summary: Japan's Fifteenth Army crosses the Chindwin to invade India. At Kohima and Imphal the besieged British and Indian garrisons hold, supplied by air, and the starving attackers are destroyed.
detail:
Mutaguchi's Operation U-Go aimed to seize the British base at Imphal and forestall an Allied offensive into Burma. From 8 March 1944 three Japanese divisions, with units of Subhas Chandra Bose's Indian National Army, crossed the Chindwin, carrying minimal supplies in the expectation of living off captured stores.

Slim pulled IV Corps back into the Imphal plain, where it was surrounded but fed and reinforced by air. To the north, Sato's 31st Division reached Kohima in early April. Its small garrison, fighting at one point across the district commissioner's tennis court, held until relieved on 18 April; the battle for the ridge went on into May. Sato, his men starving, withdrew without orders at the end of May.

On 22 June the road from Kohima to Imphal was reopened. As the monsoon broke, Mutaguchi's army disintegrated; the retreat to the Chindwin left tracks lined with the bodies of soldiers dead of hunger, dysentery and malaria. The operation was formally abandoned in early July.
significance: The largest defeat yet suffered by a Japanese army on land, it ended any threat to India and opened the way for Slim's reconquest of Burma in 1945.
uncertaintyNote: Japanese losses are estimates; most sources give c. 30,000 dead and a similar number sick or wounded. The end date varies; Mutaguchi's offensive was cancelled in early July.
sources: Robert Lyman, Japan's Last Bid for Victory: The Invasion of India 1944 (2011)
William Slim, Defeat into Victory (1956)
Christopher Bayly and Tim Harper, Forgotten Armies (2004)

title: Operation Ichi-Go
place: Henan, Hunan and Guangxi provinces, China
casualties: Chinese military casualties in the hundreds of thousands; Japanese far fewer; very large civilian losses
summary: Japan's largest offensive of the war drives south through Henan, Hunan and Guangxi, overrunning American airfields and opening a land corridor from Manchuria to Indochina.
detail:
In April 1944, with its sea lanes under American attack, the Japanese army launched Ichi-Go ('Operation Number One'), committing some half a million men. Its aims were to destroy the airfields of Chennault's Fourteenth Air Force and to link Japanese-held territory from north China to Indochina by rail.

From 17 April Japanese divisions crossed the Yellow River into Henan, a province still wrecked by the famine of 1942–43; Luoyang fell in late May, and some peasants turned on the retreating Nationalist troops. In Hunan, Changsha fell on 18 June. At Hengyang Fang Xianjue's Tenth Army held out for 47 days until 8 August, the one great stand of the campaign. Guilin and Liuzhou, with their airbases, fell in November, and by early December Japanese spearheads were in Guizhou, within reach of Guiyang and the road to Chongqing.

The offensive then halted, overextended. The Nationalist armies had lost hundreds of thousands of men, and the crisis brought a bitter breach between Chiang Kai-shek and Stilwell, who was recalled in October.
significance: Ichi-Go was Japan's last great land victory: it gravely weakened the Nationalist state and its armies, with lasting consequences for the civil war that followed, while doing little to change the course of the war at sea.
uncertaintyNote: Chinese casualty figures are uncertain and vary widely between sources; estimates of 500,000 to 750,000 killed, wounded and captured are often cited.
sources: Rana Mitter, China's War with Japan, 1937–1945: The Struggle for Survival (2013)
Hans van de Ven, China at War (2017)
Mark Peattie, Edward Drea and Hans van de Ven (eds), The Battle for China (2011)

title: Deportation of Hungary's Jews to Auschwitz
place: Hungary (including Carpathian Ruthenia and northern Transylvania), to Auschwitz-Birkenau

sides.focus: Germany (SS) and Hungary (government, gendarmerie and officials)

casualties: c. 437,000 deported in under eight weeks, most murdered in the gas chambers on arrival; c. 565,000 Hungarian Jews died in the Holocaust
summary: Two months after Germany occupies Hungary, the Hungarian gendarmerie and Eichmann's SS unit deport some 437,000 Jews to Auschwitz in eight weeks. Most are gassed on arrival.
detail:
Hungary's Jews, some 800,000 people, had suffered discriminatory laws, forced labour service and massacres, but most were still alive in March 1944. On 19 March Germany occupied its faltering ally; a new government under Sztójay placed the Hungarian state at the disposal of Adolf Eichmann's small SS team, and the Hungarian officials László Endre and László Baky organised the rest.

From April Jews were forced into ghettos and brickyards, starting in Carpathian Ruthenia and northern Transylvania. From 15 May the Hungarian gendarmerie loaded them into freight wagons, around 3,000 to a train, often four trains a day. At Birkenau a new rail spur ran into the camp; SS doctors selected a minority for labour and sent the rest to the gas chambers, whose crematoria could not keep pace.

Under pressure from the Pope, the King of Sweden and the United States, and as news of Auschwitz spread through the escapees' reports, Horthy halted the deportations in early July, before the Jews of Budapest were taken. After the Arrow Cross seized power in October, thousands more were driven on death marches or shot on the banks of the Danube.
significance: The murder of Hungarian Jewry was the last great deportation of the Holocaust, carried out at the very moment the Allies were landing in Normandy, and made Auschwitz its single largest killing site.
uncertaintyNote: The figure of c. 437,000 deported comes from German and Hungarian railway and police reports; the number killed on arrival is estimated, usually at about three-quarters. Whether and how the Allies could have bombed the railways or the camp remains debated.
sources: Randolph L. Braham, The Politics of Genocide: The Holocaust in Hungary (1981)
Saul Friedländer, The Years of Extermination (2007)
Raul Hilberg, The Destruction of the European Jews (3rd edn, 2003)
David Cesarani (ed.), Genocide and Rescue: The Holocaust in Hungary 1944 (1997)

title: Fall of Rome
place: Rome

sides.opponent: United States, Britain and the Commonwealth

summary: The Germans abandon Rome without a fight and the US Fifth Army enters the first Axis capital to fall. Clark's dash for the city lets the German Tenth Army escape north.
detail:
After the Gustav Line broke in May 1944, Alexander's plan was for VI Corps, breaking out of Anzio, to drive east to Valmontone and cut the line of retreat of the German Tenth Army. On 25 May Mark Clark turned most of the corps north-west towards Rome instead, determined that the Fifth Army, and not the British, should take the city.

Kesselring, unwilling to fight in Rome and under pressure to spare it, withdrew his armies through and around the city. American troops entered on 4 June to crowds in the streets, and Clark posed for photographers on the Capitol. The occupation had been harsh: in October 1943 more than 1,000 of Rome's Jews had been deported to Auschwitz, and in March 1944, after a partisan bomb in the Via Rasella killed 33 German police, the SS shot 335 men and boys in the Ardeatine Caves.

Rome's liberation was overshadowed within two days by the landings in Normandy, and the German armies withdrew in good order to the Gothic Line in the northern Apennines.
significance: The first Axis capital to fall to the Allies, Rome was a symbolic triumph; but the escape of the German armies meant the Italian campaign would grind on until the last days of the war.
uncertaintyNote: Whether Clark's turn towards Rome actually allowed the Tenth Army to escape, or whether Valmontone could have been held, is debated by historians.
sources: Rick Atkinson, The Day of Battle (2007)
Carlo D'Este, Fatal Decision: Anzio and the Battle for Rome (1991)
Robert Katz, The Battle for Rome (2003)

title: D-Day: the Normandy landings
place: The Calvados and Cotentin coast, Normandy, France

sides.opponent: United States, Britain, Canada and Allies

strength.opponent: c. 156,000 landed by sea and air on 6 June

casualties: Allied c. 10,000 on D-Day, including c. 4,400 dead; German perhaps 4,000–9,000
summary: Some 156,000 Allied troops land by sea and air on five Normandy beaches. By nightfall, despite carnage at Omaha, the Atlantic Wall is breached and the second front is open.
detail:
After a day's delay for weather, Operation Neptune, the assault phase of Overlord, began in the night of 5–6 June 1944. Three airborne divisions dropped to secure the flanks: the American 82nd and 101st behind Utah Beach, the British 6th east of the Orne, where gliders seized the bridges at Bénouville. At dawn some 7,000 ships and landing craft stood off the coast.

At Utah the Americans landed off course but lightly opposed. At Omaha, bluffs, intact defences and a veteran German division pinned the 1st and 29th Divisions on the beach for hours, with some 2,000 or more casualties, before small groups climbed the draws. The British at Gold and Sword and the Canadians at Juno got ashore and inland, though not as far as Caen.

The Germans were slow to react: deceived by Operation Fortitude into expecting the main blow at Calais, with Rommel away in Germany and the panzer reserves needing Hitler's release. By midnight the Allies held a broken but secure foothold. The Normandy campaign that followed cost both armies dearly and killed some 20,000 French civilians.
significance: D-Day opened the long-awaited second front in the west, the greatest amphibious operation in history, and with Bagration in the east sealed Germany's defeat.
uncertaintyNote: The D-Day casualty figures are estimates; recent research puts Allied dead at c. 4,400. German losses on the day are not known with precision.
sources: Antony Beevor, D-Day: The Battle for Normandy (2009)
Max Hastings, Overlord (1984)
Rick Atkinson, The Guns at Last Light (2013)
Carlo D'Este, Decision in Normandy (1983)

title: Massacre at Oradour-sur-Glane
place: Oradour-sur-Glane, near Limoges, Haute-Vienne, France
casualties: 642 men, women and children killed
summary: A company of the SS division Das Reich, moving north to Normandy, murders 642 inhabitants of a French village, shooting the men and burning the women and children in the church.
detail:
As the SS Panzer Division Das Reich moved north from Montauban towards Normandy in June 1944, it was harassed by the Resistance and answered with terror. On 9 June at Tulle its troops hanged 99 men from balconies and lampposts and deported many more.

On the afternoon of 10 June a company under Adolf Diekmann sealed off Oradour-sur-Glane, a village with no particular connection to the Resistance, and gathered its people on the fair ground. The men were divided among barns and garages and machine-gunned, and the buildings set on fire. The women and children were locked into the church, which was then set alight; those who tried to escape were shot. A handful of people survived. The village was looted and burned.

De Gaulle ordered the ruins preserved as they were, and they stand today beside the rebuilt village. The 1953 trial at Bordeaux, at which most of the accused were Alsatians forcibly conscripted into the SS, and the amnesty that followed, divided France bitterly.
significance: Oradour became the emblem in France of German atrocities against civilians during the occupation and the struggle for liberation.
uncertaintyNote: The death toll is given as 642 or 643. The motive is debated: reprisal for the capture of an SS officer by the Resistance, mistaken identity with another village, or simple terror.
sources: Sarah Farmer, Martyred Village: Commemorating the 1944 Massacre at Oradour-sur-Glane (1999)
Max Hastings, Das Reich (1981)

title: Battle of Saipan

markers.name: Marpi Point (the cliffs of the civilian suicides)

place: Saipan, Mariana Islands
casualties: Japanese almost the entire garrison of c. 30,000; US c. 3,400 killed, c. 13,000 wounded; perhaps 20,000 civilians dead
summary: US Marines and soldiers storm Saipan, inside Japan's inner defence line. The garrison dies almost to the last man, and thousands of Japanese civilians kill themselves rather than surrender.
detail:
Saipan, with its Japanese settler population, lay within the empire's inner perimeter and within B-29 range of Tokyo. On 15 June 1944 the 2nd and 4th Marine Divisions landed on the south-west coast under heavy fire; the Army's 27th Division followed. The approach of the Japanese fleet that week brought on the Battle of the Philippine Sea, which left the garrison without hope of relief.

The Americans fought north through mountains, cane fields and caves. The relief of the 27th Division's commander by the Marine general Holland Smith caused a lasting inter-service quarrel. On 7 July some 3,000 Japanese, soldiers, sailors and civilians, made the largest banzai charge of the Pacific war; Saito and Nagumo, the admiral of Pearl Harbor, took their own lives. The island was declared secure on 9 July.

In its final days Japanese civilians, told to expect atrocities from the Americans and in some cases pressed by soldiers, killed their families with grenades or leapt from the cliffs at Marpi Point while American interpreters pleaded with them to surrender.
significance: The loss of Saipan brought down Tojo's government and gave the United States the bases from which B-29s would burn Japan's cities.
uncertaintyNote: Civilian deaths on Saipan are estimated at c. 20,000 or more; the number who killed themselves is not known.
sources: Harold J. Goldberg, D-Day in the Pacific: The Battle of Saipan (2007)
Ronald H. Spector, Eagle Against the Sun (1985)
Max Hastings, Nemesis (2007)

title: Battle of the Philippine Sea
place: The Philippine Sea, west of the Mariana Islands
casualties: Japanese 3 carriers sunk, c. 550–600 aircraft lost; US c. 120 aircraft, many ditched at night
summary: Japan's carrier fleet sorties to save the Marianas. In the 'Marianas Turkey Shoot' its air groups are annihilated, and American submarines sink two of its largest carriers.
detail:
When the Americans landed on Saipan, the Imperial Navy committed Ozawa's Mobile Fleet in the Operation A-Go plan for a decisive battle. Ozawa's aircraft outranged the Americans', and on 19 June 1944 he launched four great raids against Mitscher's Task Force 58.

The Japanese aircrews, hastily trained replacements for the veterans lost since Midway, met radar-directed Hellcat fighters and a barrage of anti-aircraft fire. Some 300 or more aircraft fell that day for the loss of about 30 American; pilots called it the Great Marianas Turkey Shoot. The same day the submarines Albacore and Cavalla torpedoed the carriers Taiho and Shokaku, both of which blew up.

Spruance, keeping his fleet close to guard the landings, was criticised for not pursuing. Late on 20 June Mitscher launched a long-range strike that sank the carrier Hiyo; returning in darkness, low on fuel, many American aircraft ditched, and Mitscher ordered the fleet's lights switched on to guide them home.
significance: The battle destroyed Japanese naval aviation as a fighting force; at Leyte Gulf four months later Japan's surviving carriers could serve only as decoys.
uncertaintyNote: Japanese aircraft losses, including those destroyed on Guam and on the sunk carriers, are given variously from c. 550 to over 600. The battle's position spans several hundred kilometres of ocean.
sources: Samuel Eliot Morison, History of United States Naval Operations in World War II, vol. 8: New Guinea and the Marianas (1953)
Ronald H. Spector, Eagle Against the Sun (1985)
Barrett Tillman, Clash of the Carriers (2005)

title: Operation Bagration
place: Belorussia (Belarus), to the Vistula and the borders of East Prussia
casualties: German c. 400,000 killed, wounded or captured; Soviet c. 770,000, including c. 180,000 killed
summary: Three years to the day after Barbarossa, four Soviet fronts smash Army Group Centre in Belorussia. In two months the Red Army advances some 500 km to the gates of Warsaw.
detail:
The Red Army's summer offensive, named after a general of 1812, struck where the German command least expected it. Deception convinced Hitler the blow would fall in the Ukraine; partisans cut the railways behind Army Group Centre in the nights before 22 June 1944, and four fronts attacked along a 700 km line with overwhelming artillery, armour and air power.

Hitler's orders to hold 'fortified places' doomed whole corps. Vitebsk was encircled within days and Bobruisk soon after, its pocket destroyed from the air and by Rokossovsky's tanks. Minsk was retaken on 3 July, trapping more than 100,000 men east of the city. On 17 July some 57,000 German prisoners were marched through Moscow. Busch was replaced by Model, who could only slow the collapse.

By mid-August, joined by the Lvov–Sandomierz offensive to the south, Soviet armies had reached the Vistula and the East Prussian border. On 23 July they entered Majdanek, near Lublin, the first major extermination camp to be liberated. Behind them lay a Belorussia devastated by three years of occupation, in which perhaps a quarter of the population had died.
significance: Bagration destroyed Army Group Centre, the greatest single defeat in German military history, and with Normandy left the Reich facing collapse on both fronts.
uncertaintyNote: Figures for both sides' strength and losses vary considerably between German, Soviet and later scholarly accounts; the German losses given are Karl-Heinz Frieser's estimate.
sources: David M. Glantz and Jonathan M. House, When Titans Clashed (1995)
Karl-Heinz Frieser et al., Germany and the Second World War, vol. 8 (2007; Eng. trans. 2017)
Steven J. Zaloga, Bagration 1944 (1996)
Richard Overy, Russia's War (1997)

title: The 20 July plot
place: Wolfsschanze, near Rastenburg (Kętrzyn), East Prussia
casualties: 4 killed by the bomb; Stauffenberg and three others shot that night; c. 200 later executed in direct connection with the plot, thousands arrested
summary: Colonel von Stauffenberg sets off a bomb beside Hitler at his East Prussian headquarters. Hitler survives with minor injuries; the coup in Berlin collapses within hours.
detail:
A network of officers and civilians had planned for years to kill Hitler and end the war. Colonel Claus Schenk Graf von Stauffenberg, badly wounded in Tunisia and now chief of staff of the Replacement Army, had access to Hitler's briefings. On 20 July 1944, at the Wolfsschanze headquarters, he placed a briefcase bomb under the map table in a wooden briefing hut and left on a pretext. It exploded at about 12.42, killing four men, but the heavy table and the open windows shielded Hitler.

Stauffenberg flew back to Berlin believing Hitler dead. At the Bendlerblock the conspirators launched Operation Valkyrie, a plan to mobilise the reserve army against the SS, but they had lost hours, and the news that Hitler lived turned waverers back to loyalty. That night General Fromm had Stauffenberg, Olbricht and two others shot in the courtyard; Beck was allowed to attempt suicide.

The Gestapo's investigation reached far beyond the plotters. Many were tried before Roland Freisler's People's Court and hanged; Rommel, implicated, was forced to take poison in October.
significance: The plot's failure tightened the Nazi grip on the army for the war's last ten months; its participants later became symbols of the 'other Germany' in the Federal Republic.
uncertaintyNote: There is no Axis-versus-Allied outcome here, so 'n/a'. Figures for those executed after the plot range from c. 200 directly involved to several thousand when the wider purge is included.
sources: Peter Hoffmann, The History of the German Resistance 1933–1945 (1977)
Ian Kershaw, Hitler 1936–1945: Nemesis (2000)
Joachim Fest, Plotting Hitler's Death (1996)

title: Normandy breakout and the Falaise pocket
place: Between Saint-Lô, Falaise and Chambois, Normandy

sides.opponent: United States, Britain, Canada and Poland

casualties: In the pocket, German c. 10,000 dead and c. 50,000 captured; tens of thousands more escaped without their heavy equipment
summary: American armies break out west of Saint-Lô and swing east. Hitler's counter-attack at Mortain drives the German armies into a trap, and the Falaise pocket closes on them.
detail:
For seven weeks the Allies were held in the Normandy bocage, while British and Canadian attacks around Caen drew most of the German armour. On 25 July 1944, after carpet bombing that also killed many American soldiers, Bradley's Operation Cobra broke through west of Saint-Lô. Patton's newly activated Third Army poured through the gap at Avranches into Brittany and turned east.

Instead of retreating, Hitler ordered a counter-attack towards Avranches, which was stopped at Mortain on 7 August. The German Seventh Army and Fifth Panzer Army were now in a sack, with Americans closing from the south and Canadians and Poles from the north towards Falaise. Kluge, under suspicion after 20 July, was relieved and took poison.

The pocket was sealed between Trun and Chambois on 19–21 August, with the Polish 1st Armoured Division holding Hill 262 at Mont Ormel against desperate breakout attempts. Allied aircraft and artillery turned the roads of the pocket into a slaughterhouse of men, horses and vehicles.
significance: The Falaise pocket wrecked the German armies in the west and opened the road to Paris and the Seine.
uncertaintyNote: The number of Germans who escaped the pocket before it closed is disputed, with estimates from c. 20,000 to over 50,000.
sources: Antony Beevor, D-Day: The Battle for Normandy (2009)
Max Hastings, Overlord (1984)
Carlo D'Este, Decision in Normandy (1983)

title: Warsaw Uprising
place: Warsaw
casualties: Insurgents c. 16,000 killed; civilians c. 150,000–200,000; Germans several thousand to c. 17,000
summary: As the Red Army nears, the Polish Home Army rises in Warsaw. The Soviets halt on the Vistula; for 63 days the insurgents fight alone, and the Germans massacre civilians and then raze the city.
detail:
On 1 August 1944 the Home Army, loyal to the Polish government in London, rose in Warsaw to free the capital before the Red Army arrived. It seized much of the centre but failed to take the bridges, the airfield or the main German strongpoints, and many fighters had no weapons at all.

Himmler ordered the city wiped out. SS and police units under Bach-Zelewski, among them the Dirlewanger and Kaminski brigades, murdered perhaps 40,000 civilians in the district of Wola in the first days of August. The insurgents fought on from district to district, moving through the sewers when the Old Town fell in early September.

The Soviet armies, checked east of the river in early August, did not renew their advance until mid-September, when they took the suburb of Praga; Stalin had refused Allied supply aircraft the use of Soviet airfields until then, and RAF, Polish and South African crews flying from Italy suffered heavy losses. The Home Army capitulated on 2 October with combatant rights. The survivors were expelled, and German demolition squads then burned and blew up most of what remained of the city.
significance: The uprising's destruction removed the non-communist Polish underground as a force before the Soviet occupation, and the fate of Warsaw became a lasting grievance in Poland's memory of the war.
uncertaintyNote: Whether the Red Army could have helped in August, or chose not to, remains bitterly disputed. Civilian death estimates vary; German military losses are especially uncertain.
sources: Norman Davies, Rising '44: The Battle for Warsaw (2003)
Alexandra Richie, Warsaw 1944 (2013)
Włodzimierz Borodziej, The Warsaw Uprising of 1944 (2001; Eng. trans. 2006)

title: Operation Dragoon
place: The Côte d'Azur between Cavalaire and Saint-Raphaël, Provence, France
casualties: German c. 130,000 captured over the campaign; Allied losses comparatively light
summary: American and French forces land on the Riviera. The French take Toulon and Marseille, and the German army in southern France retreats up the Rhône to escape encirclement.
detail:
Long argued over by the Allies, with Churchill pressing for operations in Italy and the Balkans instead, the landing in southern France went in on 15 August 1944. Three American divisions of Truscott's VI Corps came ashore between Cavalaire and Saint-Raphaël after airborne drops inland, meeting light resistance; French Army B under de Lattre followed.

The German Nineteenth Army, stripped of units for Normandy, could not hold the coast. Hitler ordered a withdrawal from most of southern and south-western France, leaving garrisons in the great ports. French troops, many of them from North and West Africa, fought their way into Toulon and Marseille and took both by 28 August, far ahead of schedule. An American task force raced north to cut off the retreat at Montélimar but could not close the trap.

On 12 September Dragoon forces met patrols of Patton's Third Army west of Dijon, uniting the two Allied fronts in France.
significance: Dragoon cleared southern France in a month and gave the Allies the port of Marseille, which became a principal supply line for the armies in the west.
uncertaintyNote: Prisoner totals for the campaign vary with how the retreat through France is counted.
sources: Rick Atkinson, The Guns at Last Light (2013)
Jeffrey J. Clarke and Robert Ross Smith, Riviera to the Rhine (US Army official history, 1993)

title: Liberation of Paris
place: Paris

sides.opponent: Free French and French Resistance, United States

casualties: French Resistance and civilians c. 1,500–2,000 killed; German c. 3,000 killed and c. 10,000 captured; figures approximate
summary: Paris rises against its occupiers, and Leclerc's French armoured division enters the city. General von Choltitz surrenders on 25 August, and de Gaulle speaks at the Hôtel de Ville.
detail:
Eisenhower had planned to bypass Paris, but on 19 August 1944 the city's police occupied the Préfecture and the Resistance, under the communist Henri Rol-Tanguy, began building barricades. A fragile truce, brokered by the Swedish consul, broke down. De Gaulle pressed Eisenhower to send in French troops, fearing both a massacre and a communist seizure of power.

Leclerc's 2nd Armoured Division, with the American 4th Infantry Division alongside, pushed in from the south-west; on the night of 24 August a small column reached the Hôtel de Ville. The next day French tanks fought German strongpoints across the city, and the commandant, General Dietrich von Choltitz, surrendered at the Préfecture and then the Gare Montparnasse. Hitler had ordered that Paris not fall into Allied hands except as a field of ruins; Choltitz did not carry out the demolitions.

That evening de Gaulle spoke of Paris liberated by itself, with the help of all France, and on 26 August he walked down the Champs-Élysées before vast crowds.
significance: The liberation of Paris restored the capital to France without its destruction and confirmed de Gaulle as the head of a provisional government recognised at home and, soon, abroad.
uncertaintyNote: How far Choltitz deliberately saved the city, as he later claimed, or was simply unable to destroy it, is debated. Casualty figures vary.
sources: Antony Beevor and Artemis Cooper, Paris After the Liberation 1944–1949 (1994)
Julian Jackson, France: The Dark Years 1940–1944 (2001)
Rick Atkinson, The Guns at Last Light (2013)

title: Romania changes sides
place: Bucharest, after the Jassy–Kishinev offensive

sides.opponent: Romania (King Michael) and the Soviet Union

casualties: In the Jassy–Kishinev offensive, German and Romanian losses of several hundred thousand, most of them captured
summary: As Soviet armies break the front in Moldavia, King Michael has Marshal Antonescu arrested and takes Romania out of the Axis. Germany loses its main oil supply and its southern front collapses.
detail:
On 20 August 1944 Malinovsky's and Tolbukhin's fronts attacked Army Group South Ukraine at Jassy and Kishinev, and within days the rebuilt German Sixth Army was encircled and destroyed, the second army of that name lost in two years. Romanian divisions gave way or stopped fighting.

On 23 August the young King Michael summoned the dictator Ion Antonescu to the palace and had him arrested, announcing that Romania accepted the Allies' armistice terms. German aircraft bombed Bucharest in reprisal, and on 25 August Romania declared war on Germany; its troops cleared the capital of German forces. The Red Army entered Bucharest on 31 August, and the Ploiești oilfields, the Reich's chief source of natural oil, were lost.

Antonescu's regime had been a full partner in the war against the Soviet Union and in the murder of Jews and Roma in Bessarabia, Bukovina and Transnistria; he was tried and executed in 1946. Bulgaria, invaded by the Soviets in early September, changed sides within days.
significance: Romania's defection collapsed the German position in the Balkans, opened Bulgaria, Yugoslavia and Hungary to the Red Army and cut off Germany's oil from Ploiești.
uncertaintyNote: German losses in the offensive are estimated variously; Soviet sources claimed over 200,000 prisoners. The event is placed at Bucharest on the date of the coup.
sources: David M. Glantz and Jonathan M. House, When Titans Clashed (1995)
Dennis Deletant, Hitler's Forgotten Ally: Ion Antonescu and His Regime (2006)
Gerhard L. Weinberg, A World at Arms (1994)

title: Slovak National Uprising
place: Central Slovakia, centred on Banská Bystrica
casualties: Thousands of insurgents killed; reprisals killed several thousand civilians, and thousands of Jews were deported
summary: Units of the Slovak army and partisans rise against the pro-German Tiso regime. German forces close in, and the Soviet attempt to break through the Dukla Pass comes too late.
detail:
Slovakia had been a German client state under Jozef Tiso since 1939. In 1944 officers of its army, with democratic and communist resistance groups, prepared a rising timed to coincide with a Soviet advance across the Carpathians. When German troops entered the country at the end of August to suppress partisan activity, the insurgents proclaimed the uprising on 29 August from Banská Bystrica.

Two divisions in eastern Slovakia that were meant to open the passes to the Red Army were disarmed by the Germans in a day. The insurgents held a pocket in central Slovakia for two months, supplied by Soviet aircraft and joined by a Czechoslovak parachute brigade. The Soviet and Czechoslovak offensive through the Dukla Pass in September and October cost very heavy losses and broke through only after the rising had been crushed.

Banská Bystrica fell on 27 October; the commanders Golian and Viest were captured and died in German hands. SS and police units carried out mass shootings, notably at Kremnička and Nemecká, and the deportations of Slovakia's remaining Jews resumed.
significance: Though defeated, the uprising became a founding event of post-war Czechoslovakia and of modern Slovakia's memory of the war.
uncertaintyNote: Figures for insurgent strength and losses and for the victims of reprisals vary between sources.
sources: Gerhard L. Weinberg, A World at Arms (1994)
Jozef Jablonický, Povstanie bez legiend (1990)
Mark Cornwall and R.J.W. Evans (eds), Czechoslovakia in a Nationalist and Fascist Europe 1918–1948 (2007)

title: The V-2 rocket campaign
place: London, Antwerp and their surroundings, launched from the Netherlands and Germany
casualties: c. 2,700 killed in Britain and c. 1,700 or more in Antwerp by V-2s; c. 6,000 killed in Britain by V-1s; at least 10,000 prisoners died building the weapons
summary: Germany fires the first ballistic missiles in history at London and Antwerp. Falling faster than sound, without warning, the V-2s kill thousands of civilians but cannot change the war.
detail:
Germany's 'vengeance weapons' were launched against cities. The V-1 flying bomb, first fired at London on 13 June 1944, killed some 6,000 people in Britain before its launching sites were overrun, though many were shot down by fighters and guns. The V-2, a liquid-fuelled rocket carrying a tonne of explosive, could not be intercepted at all. The first struck Paris and then Chiswick, in west London, on 8 September 1944.

From mobile launchers in the Netherlands, more than 1,000 V-2s fell on England and some 1,600 on Antwerp, the Allies' vital supply port. On 25 November one hit a Woolworths store in New Cross, killing 168 people; on 16 December another struck the Rex cinema in Antwerp, killing over 500, many of them soldiers. The last V-2 to land in England, on 27 March 1945, killed 134 people in a block of flats in Stepney.

The rockets were assembled in the tunnels of the Mittelwerk in the Harz mountains by prisoners of the Mittelbau-Dora camp, where more people died making the weapon than were killed by it.
significance: The V-2 was a technological landmark, the ancestor of the ballistic missile and the space rocket, and a costly strategic failure that diverted German resources and killed civilians to no military effect.
uncertaintyNote: Death tolls are approximate and vary between British, Belgian and German sources; estimates of prisoner deaths in V-2 production range from c. 10,000 to 20,000.
sources: Michael J. Neufeld, The Rocket and the Reich (1995)
Richard Overy, The Bombing War (2013)
Jens-Christian Wagner, Produktion des Todes: Das KZ Mittelbau-Dora (2001)

title: Battle of Peleliu
place: Peleliu, Palau Islands

strength.opponent: 1st Marine Division and the Army's 81st Infantry Division, c. 47,000 men

casualties: Japanese c. 10,700 dead and some 200 captured; US c. 1,800 killed and 8,000 wounded
summary: US Marines land on Peleliu expecting a four-day fight and face ten weeks of slaughter against Japanese troops dug into coral ridges.
detail:
Peleliu's airfield was meant to cover MacArthur's flank for the return to the Philippines. Rupertus predicted a quick, rough fight. But Colonel Nakagawa, under new Japanese doctrine, did not try to stop the landing at the water's edge. He fortified the caves of the Umurbrogol ridges above the airfield, hundreds of them, linked and mutually supporting, and fought a battle of attrition from them.

The Marines took the airfield in the first days in heat of over 40°C, then were fed into the ridges, 'Bloody Nose Ridge', where the 1st Marine Regiment lost more than half its men in a week. The Army's 81st Division took over in October and reduced the pocket cave by cave with flamethrowers and demolitions. Nakagawa burned his regimental colours and killed himself on 24 November; the last organised resistance ended on 27 November.
significance: Peleliu was among the costliest battles of the Pacific war in proportion to the forces engaged, of doubtful strategic value, and the first full use of the cave-based defence the Japanese would repeat on Iwo Jima and Okinawa.
uncertaintyNote: A few Japanese soldiers held out in the caves until 1947.
sources: Eugene B. Sledge, With the Old Breed: At Peleliu and Okinawa (1981)
Bill Sloan, Brotherhood of Heroes: The Marines at Peleliu, 1944 (2005)
Ian W. Toll, Twilight of the Gods: War in the Western Pacific, 1944–1945 (2020)

title: Operation Market Garden
place: The road from the Belgian border through Eindhoven and Nijmegen to Arnhem, the Netherlands
casualties: Allied c. 15,000–17,000; British 1st Airborne Division lost c. 1,500 killed and over 6,000 captured; German c. 3,000–8,000
summary: Three airborne divisions drop to seize the bridges to Arnhem for a dash across the Rhine. The ground advance stalls short of the last bridge, and the British paratroops at Arnhem are destroyed.
detail:
Montgomery's plan was audacious: the American 101st and 82nd Airborne Divisions would seize the canal and river bridges at Eindhoven, Grave and Nijmegen, and the British 1st Airborne, with a Polish brigade, the Rhine bridge at Arnhem, while Horrocks's XXX Corps drove 100 km up a single road to join them. Success might end the war by Christmas.

The drops began on 17 September 1944. The landing zones at Arnhem lay far from the town, and II SS Panzer Corps, refitting nearby, reacted fast. Only Lt-Col John Frost's battalion reached the north end of the bridge, which it held until 21 September. XXX Corps was delayed by a blown bridge at Son and fighting along the exposed road; the Nijmegen bridge fell only on 20 September, after American paratroopers crossed the Waal in canvas boats under fire.

The rest of 1st Airborne was squeezed into a perimeter at Oosterbeek. On the night of 25–26 September some 2,400 survivors were ferried back across the Rhine. Dutch support for the operation was punished: a German embargo on food transport helped bring on the Hunger Winter, in which some 20,000 people died.
significance: Market Garden's failure ended hopes of finishing the war in 1944 and left the Allies with a narrow salient, while the port of Antwerp remained unusable until November.
uncertaintyNote: German casualty figures are uncertain. Hunger Winter deaths are commonly put at c. 18,000–22,000.
sources: Antony Beevor, Arnhem: The Battle for the Bridges, 1944 (2018)
Cornelius Ryan, A Bridge Too Far (1974)
Martin Middlebrook, Arnhem 1944: The Airborne Battle (1994)

title: Battle of the Scheldt
place: The Scheldt estuary, between Antwerp and the North Sea, Netherlands and Belgium

strength.focus: Elements of 15th Army, including the 64th and 70th Infantry Divisions, c. 90,000 men
strength.opponent: First Canadian Army with British, Polish and other Allied units, and commandos for Walcheren

casualties: Allied c. 12,900 killed, wounded and missing, half of them Canadian; c. 41,000 Germans captured
summary: The First Canadian Army fights for five weeks through flooded polders to clear the banks of the Scheldt, opening the port of Antwerp to Allied shipping.
detail:
The British had taken Antwerp intact on 4 September 1944, but the port was useless while the Germans held the 80-kilometre estuary leading to it. Montgomery gave priority to Market Garden, and the German 15th Army escaped across the estuary and dug in. The task of clearing it fell to the First Canadian Army under Guy Simonds.

The battle opened on 2 October. The Canadians attacked across the Leopold Canal into the Breskens pocket on the south bank, through polders where the only dry ground was on the dykes. North of Antwerp they fought for the neck of South Beveland and the causeway to Walcheren. RAF Bomber Command breached Walcheren's sea dykes to flood the island, and on 1 November British commandos and Canadian troops landed at Flushing and Westkapelle. Resistance ended on 8 November. After the estuary was swept of mines, the first convoy reached Antwerp on 28 November.
significance: Opening Antwerp solved the Allies' supply crisis in the west and made possible the advance into Germany in 1945; the delay in clearing it was one of the costliest Allied mistakes of 1944.
sources: Terry Copp, Cinderella Army: The Canadians in Northwest Europe, 1944–1945 (2006)
Mark Zuehlke, Terrible Victory: First Canadian Army and the Scheldt Estuary Campaign (2007)
Max Hastings, Armageddon: The Battle for Germany 1944–45 (2004)

title: Battle of Leyte Gulf
place: The seas around Leyte and Samar, the Philippines
casualties: Japanese 4 carriers, 3 battleships, 10 cruisers and c. 11 destroyers sunk, over 10,000 dead; US 1 light carrier, 2 escort carriers and 3 destroyers or escorts sunk, c. 3,000 dead
summary: Japan throws its whole remaining fleet at the American landings on Leyte. In four days of battles across the Philippine seas, the Imperial Navy is broken; the first kamikaze attacks begin.
detail:
On 20 October 1944 MacArthur's Sixth Army landed on Leyte. Japan's Sho-Go plan sent almost every remaining warship against it: Ozawa's carriers, with few aircraft, would lure Halsey's Third Fleet north, while two battleship forces converged on the landing beaches.

On 24 October American carrier aircraft caught Kurita's Centre Force in the Sibuyan Sea and sank the giant battleship Musashi; Kurita turned back, and Halsey, believing him beaten, took his whole fleet north after Ozawa. That night Nishimura's Southern Force steamed into Surigao Strait and was destroyed by Oldendorf's old battleships, several of them salvaged from Pearl Harbor, in the last battleship action in history.

At dawn on 25 October Kurita, having turned again through the unguarded San Bernardino Strait, fell on Taffy 3, a group of escort carriers and destroyers off Samar. The destroyers' suicidal torpedo attacks and the aircraft of the escort carriers confused him, and he withdrew within reach of the transports. Off Cape Engaño, Halsey's aircraft sank all four of Ozawa's carriers. The same day, the first organised kamikaze attacks sank the escort carrier St. Lo.
significance: Perhaps the largest naval battle in history, Leyte Gulf destroyed the Japanese navy as a fleet and sealed the reconquest of the Philippines; from then on Japan relied increasingly on suicide tactics.
uncertaintyNote: Losses depend on whether ships sunk in the days after the main actions are counted. The battle covered a huge area; the point shown is central, with markers for the main actions.
sources: Samuel Eliot Morison, History of United States Naval Operations in World War II, vol. 12: Leyte (1958)
H.P. Willmott, The Battle of Leyte Gulf: The Last Fleet Action (2005)
Ronald H. Spector, Eagle Against the Sun (1985)
James D. Hornfischer, The Last Stand of the Tin Can Sailors (2004)

title: Sinking of the Tirpitz
place: Håkøya, near Tromsø, Norway

strength.focus: Battleship Tirpitz, moored as a floating battery
strength.opponent: c. 30 Lancasters of 9 and 617 Squadrons with 5.4-ton Tallboy bombs

casualties: c. 950–1,000 of Tirpitz's crew killed; no British aircraft lost
summary: RAF Lancasters armed with Tallboy earthquake bombs capsize the battleship Tirpitz in a fjord near Tromsø, ending a three-year hunt.
detail:
From her Norwegian anchorages Tirpitz, Bismarck's sister ship, had tied down much of the Home Fleet simply by existing: the fear of her had scattered convoy PQ 17 in 1942. British midget submarines crippled her in Kåfjord in September 1943, and carrier aircraft hit her repeatedly in 1944. In September 1944 Lancasters flying from a Soviet airfield damaged her bow with a Tallboy, and the Germans moved her south to Tromsø to serve as a floating battery against an Allied invasion of Norway.

That put her within reach of Lancasters flying from Scotland. On the morning of 12 November, in clear weather and with no German fighters appearing, the bombers of 9 and 617 Squadrons hit her with at least two Tallboys. A magazine exploded and Tirpitz rolled over within minutes. Hundreds of men were trapped inside her upturned hull; rescuers cut 87 out through the bottom.
significance: The loss of Tirpitz removed the last German battleship from the war and freed British capital ships for the Far East.
uncertaintyNote: Estimates of the dead range from about 940 to over 1,200; most recent accounts give roughly 950–1,000.
sources: Patrick Bishop, Target Tirpitz (2012)
John Sweetman, Tirpitz: Hunting the Beast (2000)
Stephen Roskill, The War at Sea 1939–1945, vol. III, part 2 (1961)

title: Battle of the Bulge
place: The Ardennes, Belgium and Luxembourg

strength.opponent: c. 230,000 at the outset, rising to over 600,000

casualties: US c. 75,000–80,000 (c. 19,000 killed); German c. 80,000–100,000; British c. 1,400; c. 3,000 Belgian and Luxembourg civilians killed
summary: Hitler's last great gamble in the west: three German armies burst through the thinly held Ardennes towards Antwerp. Held at St Vith and Bastogne, they are stopped short of the Meuse.
detail:
Hitler planned the offensive himself: a surprise attack in winter weather that would ground Allied aircraft, cross the Meuse and take Antwerp, splitting the British from the Americans. On 16 December 1944 some 200,000 men of Dietrich's Sixth SS Panzer Army and Manteuffel's Fifth Panzer Army struck four American divisions, some untried, others resting, along the Ardennes front.

The northern shoulder held on the Elsenborn ridge. At St Vith a scratch American force delayed the Germans until 21 December, and at Bastogne the 101st Airborne and armoured units, surrounded, refused a demand to surrender with the reply 'Nuts!'. Patton turned his Third Army north in a few days and broke through to Bastogne on 26 December. Kampfgruppe Peiper's SS troops murdered American prisoners at Baugnez near Malmedy and Belgian civilians at Stavelot.

When the skies cleared on 23 December, Allied air power struck the German columns, whose spearheads ran out of fuel near Dinant, short of the Meuse. Through January, Allied counter-attacks pushed in the bulge in bitter cold.
significance: The largest battle fought by the US Army in the war, the Ardennes offensive used up Germany's last armoured reserves in the west and opened the way for the Allied advance to the Rhine.
uncertaintyNote: Casualty figures vary considerably between the US official history, German records and later studies.
sources: Antony Beevor, Ardennes 1944: Hitler's Last Gamble (2015)
Hugh M. Cole, The Ardennes: Battle of the Bulge (US Army official history, 1965)
Charles B. MacDonald, A Time for Trumpets (1985)

title: Siege of Budapest
place: Budapest
casualties: Civilians c. 38,000; Axis c. 100,000 killed, wounded or captured; Soviet and Romanian losses also very heavy
summary: The Red Army encircles Budapest, which Hitler orders held as a fortress. Fifty days of street fighting, with the city's people trapped in cellars, end in a doomed breakout from Buda.
detail:
In October 1944, as Horthy sought an armistice, the Germans had installed the Arrow Cross leader Ferenc Szálasi; his militias murdered thousands of Budapest's Jews over the winter, many on the Danube embankment, while diplomats such as Raoul Wallenberg tried to protect others. On 26 December Soviet and Romanian forces closed the ring around the city, trapping some 80,000 German and Hungarian troops and around 800,000 civilians.

Hitler forbade a breakout and launched three relief operations from the west, all of which failed. Pest, the flat eastern half, fell on 18 January 1945 after fighting from block to block; the Germans blew the Danube bridges behind them. In hilly Buda the defenders held the castle district until, starving, they tried to break out on the night of 11 February. Few of the tens of thousands who tried reached the German lines. Organised resistance ended on 13 February.

The city was left in ruins, and Soviet troops committed widespread looting and rape against its people.
significance: One of the longest and bloodiest city sieges of the war, Budapest consumed German forces needed elsewhere and opened the road to Vienna.
uncertaintyNote: Casualty figures are uncertain; those given follow Krisztián Ungváry's study.
sources: Krisztián Ungváry, Battle for Budapest: 100 Days in World War II (1998; Eng. trans. 2003)
David M. Glantz and Jonathan M. House, When Titans Clashed (1995)

title: Vistula–Oder offensive
place: Poland from the Vistula to the Oder
casualties: Soviet c. 194,000, including c. 43,000 killed; German losses very heavy, including many tens of thousands captured
summary: Zhukov and Konev burst out of their bridgeheads on the Vistula and in three weeks race 500 km across Poland to the Oder, less than 80 km from Berlin.
detail:
Brought forward at Churchill's request to relieve pressure in the Ardennes, the Soviet winter offensive opened on 12 January 1945, when Konev's 1st Ukrainian Front attacked out of the Sandomierz bridgehead; Zhukov's 1st Belorussian Front followed on the 14th. Against German forces outnumbered several times over, the tank armies broke into open country within days.

Warsaw, a ruined and largely empty city, fell on 17 January; Kraków was taken intact on the 19th; Łódź, Poznań's surroundings and the industrial region of Upper Silesia followed. To the north, the East Prussian offensive cut off that province, and millions of German civilians fled west in midwinter, by road, across the frozen lagoon and by sea; the sinking of the liner Wilhelm Gustloff on 30 January killed some 9,000. Soviet troops entering Germany committed mass rape and killing.

By the end of January Zhukov's spearheads had reached the Oder at Küstrin and seized bridgeheads on its west bank. There, exhausted and outrunning their supplies, they halted.
significance: The fastest advance of the war on the Eastern Front brought the Red Army within striking distance of Berlin and took the last German industrial region outside the Ruhr.
uncertaintyNote: Soviet losses are Krivosheev's official figures; German losses were never fully counted.
sources: David M. Glantz and Jonathan M. House, When Titans Clashed (1995)
Antony Beevor, Berlin: The Downfall 1945 (2002)
Ian Kershaw, The End: Germany 1944–45 (2011)

title: Liberation of Auschwitz
place: Auschwitz (Oświęcim), annexed Upper Silesia, Poland

sides.opponent: Prisoners of Auschwitz; Soviet Union (60th Army)

casualties: c. 1.1 million people murdered at Auschwitz, about 1 million of them Jews; c. 7,000 prisoners found alive at liberation
summary: Soviet soldiers enter Auschwitz and find some 7,000 sick and starving prisoners. The SS has driven the rest west on death marches and tried to destroy the evidence of the largest murder site in history.
detail:
Auschwitz grew from a concentration camp for Polish prisoners into a vast complex of camps, including the extermination centre at Birkenau, where from 1942 Jews were brought from across Europe and most were murdered in gas chambers on arrival. About 1.1 million people were killed there: around a million Jews, and also Poles, Roma, Soviet prisoners of war and others.

As the Red Army approached in January 1945, the SS blew up the crematoria and burned records. Between 17 and 21 January some 56,000 or more prisoners were marched west through snow towards camps in the Reich, and many thousands were shot or died on the roads. About 7,000 prisoners too weak to walk were left behind.

On the afternoon of 27 January soldiers of the Soviet 60th Army reached the main camp, Birkenau and Monowitz. They found survivors near death, hundreds of corpses, and in the storehouses hundreds of thousands of garments and some seven tonnes of human hair. Soviet and Polish medical teams tried to save the survivors; many died in the following weeks.
significance: Auschwitz became the central symbol of the Holocaust; 27 January is now International Holocaust Remembrance Day.
uncertaintyNote: The atlas treats this as an atrocity site rather than a battle, so 'n/a'. The death toll follows Franciszek Piper's research for the Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum; earlier Soviet claims of 4 million were wrong.
sources: Yisrael Gutman and Michael Berenbaum (eds), Anatomy of the Auschwitz Death Camp (1994)
Danuta Czech, Auschwitz Chronicle 1939–1945 (1990)
Nikolaus Wachsmann, KL: A History of the Nazi Concentration Camps (2015)
Laurence Rees, Auschwitz: The Nazis and the 'Final Solution' (2005)

title: Sinking of the Wilhelm Gustloff
place: Baltic Sea off Stolpmünde, Pomerania (Ustka, Poland)

strength.focus: Liner Wilhelm Gustloff, with c. 10,000 refugees, wounded, naval personnel and women auxiliaries aboard, and a single torpedo boat escort

casualties: c. 9,000 dead, most of them refugees, among them some 5,000 children; c. 1,250 rescued
summary: A Soviet submarine torpedoes the overcrowded liner Wilhelm Gustloff evacuating refugees from East Prussia, in the deadliest ship sinking in history.
detail:
As the Red Army cut off East Prussia in January 1945, the German navy began Operation Hannibal, the evacuation by sea of soldiers, wounded and civilians from the Baltic ports. The former Strength Through Joy cruise liner Wilhelm Gustloff, used as a barracks ship for U-boat trainees, left Gotenhafen on 30 January crammed with some 10,000 people, mostly refugees from East and West Prussia, as well as wounded soldiers, naval personnel and auxiliaries.

That night, in a snowstorm and with her navigation lights on for fear of collision, she was sighted by the Soviet submarine S-13 under Alexander Marinesko, who hit her with three torpedoes. The ship sank in about an hour in water near freezing. Lifeboats were frozen in their davits, and most of those who reached the sea died of the cold within minutes. Marinesko sank the General von Steuben, with some 4,000 aboard, ten days later.

Operation Hannibal brought out hundreds of thousands of people by sea in the last months of the war.
significance: The sinking became for many Germans the emblem of the suffering of the expellees from the east, long a muted subject in postwar Germany.
uncertaintyNote: No full passenger list survived; estimates of the dead range from about 5,300 to over 9,000, with the higher figures from Heinz Schön's research now usually accepted.
sources: Cathryn J. Prince, Death in the Baltic: The World War II Sinking of the Wilhelm Gustloff (2013)
Antony Beevor, Berlin: The Downfall 1945 (2002)
Ian Kershaw, The End: Hitler's Germany 1944–45 (2011)

title: Battle of Manila
place: Manila, Luzon, the Philippines
casualties: Filipino civilians c. 100,000; Japanese c. 16,000; US c. 1,000 killed and c. 5,500 wounded
summary: Japanese naval troops refuse to abandon Manila and fight the Americans street by street. In a month of battle and massacre some 100,000 civilians die, and the old city is destroyed.
detail:
When the Americans landed on Luzon in January 1945, Yamashita planned to defend the mountains and leave Manila. But Rear-Admiral Iwabuchi Sanji's naval troops, some 16,000 men, stayed to fight, destroying the port and fortifying the city's concrete buildings and the walled Spanish town of Intramuros.

American troops entered on 3 February and freed internees at Santo Tomas university. The battle that followed was fought building by building. MacArthur forbade bombing, but artillery was used in quantity, and much of the city was destroyed. As they were cornered, Japanese troops massacred civilians in churches, hospitals and homes, raped women and girls, and set whole districts on fire; these crimes later figured in Yamashita's trial and execution.

Intramuros was stormed in late February, and the last resistance ended on 3 March. Iwabuchi died in the fighting. Manila was, after Warsaw, among the most thoroughly destroyed Allied capitals of the war.
significance: The battle cost the lives of a large part of Manila's population and much of its heritage, and remains a central memory of the war in the Philippines.
uncertaintyNote: The civilian toll of c. 100,000 is the commonly cited estimate; how many died at Japanese hands and how many from American shelling cannot be precisely separated.
sources: Richard Connaughton, John Pimlott and Duncan Anderson, The Battle for Manila (1995)
James M. Scott, Rampage: MacArthur, Yamashita, and the Battle of Manila (2018)
Max Hastings, Nemesis (2007)

title: Yalta Conference
place: Livadia Palace, Yalta, Crimea
summary: Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin meet in the Crimea to settle the shape of the post-war world: the occupation of Germany, Poland's borders and government, the United Nations and Soviet entry into the war with Japan.
detail:
The 'Big Three' met at the former tsarist palace of Livadia from 4 to 11 February 1945, with Soviet armies on the Oder and the Western Allies recovering from the Ardennes. Roosevelt, visibly ill, sought above all Soviet participation in the war against Japan and in a United Nations organisation; Churchill fought for France's place and for Poland.

The conference agreed that Germany would be occupied in zones, with a French zone carved from the British and American ones, disarmed and made to pay reparations. Poland's eastern border would follow roughly the Curzon Line, with compensation in the west, and the communist-led provisional government would be 'reorganised' and hold free elections. A Declaration on Liberated Europe promised democratic governments chosen by the people. In a secret agreement Stalin undertook to enter the war against Japan within two or three months of Germany's surrender, in return for southern Sakhalin, the Kuril Islands and rights in Manchuria.

The agreements also provided for the return of Soviet citizens, which led to the forced repatriation of many who did not wish to go.
significance: Yalta set much of the post-war settlement in Europe and Asia; its promises on Poland and Eastern Europe were not kept, and it became a byword in the West for the division of Europe.
uncertaintyNote: No Axis power took part, so the slots hold the Soviet Union and the Western Allies, and the outcome is 'n/a'. How far Yalta 'gave away' Eastern Europe, already occupied by the Red Army, remains debated.
sources: S.M. Plokhy, Yalta: The Price of Peace (2010)
Gerhard L. Weinberg, A World at Arms (1994)
Herbert Feis, Churchill, Roosevelt, Stalin (1957)

title: Bombing of Dresden
place: Dresden, Saxony

sides.opponent: Britain and the United States (RAF Bomber Command and US Eighth Air Force)

summary: Two night raids by RAF Bomber Command and daylight attacks by American bombers raise a firestorm in Dresden. Up to 25,000 people die, many of them refugees, in one of the war's most controversial raids.
detail:
Dresden, a baroque city on the Elbe, had been little bombed and was crowded with refugees fleeing the Red Army. It was also a rail junction and an industrial centre, and at Yalta the Soviets had asked for attacks on communications behind the German front.

On the night of 13–14 February 1945 about 800 RAF Lancasters attacked in two waves, the second timed to catch rescuers in the open. High explosive and incendiaries started a firestorm that sucked the air from shelters and burned out the old city. The next day more than 300 American B-17s bombed the rail yards, and they returned on 15 February.

Nazi propaganda multiplied the death toll tenfold and more, and inflated figures circulated for decades. A commission of historians appointed by the city concluded in 2010 that up to 25,000 people had been killed. In March Churchill himself questioned the bombing of German cities 'simply for the sake of increasing the terror'.
significance: Dresden became the emblem of the moral debate over the Allied area-bombing of cities, which killed several hundred thousand German civilians.
uncertaintyNote: This is an Allied raid, not an Axis action; following the atlas convention the city's side appears as 'focus' and the outcome is 'n/a'. Death tolls of 135,000 or more, long cited, derive from Nazi propaganda and are rejected by historians.
sources: Frederick Taylor, Dresden: Tuesday 13 February 1945 (2004)
Richard Overy, The Bombing War: Europe 1939–1945 (2013)
Rolf-Dieter Müller, Nicole Schönherr and Thomas Widera (eds), Die Zerstörung Dresdens (2010)

title: Battle of Iwo Jima
place: Iwo Jima, Volcano Islands
casualties: Japanese c. 18,000–19,000 killed, c. 216 captured; US c. 26,000, including c. 6,800 killed
summary: Three Marine divisions storm a small volcanic island honeycombed with tunnels. A flag rises over Mount Suribachi on the fifth day, but the fighting lasts five weeks and costs more American casualties than Japanese.
detail:
Iwo Jima, eight square miles of volcanic ash and rock midway between the Marianas and Tokyo, was wanted as an emergency field for B-29s and a base for escort fighters. Its commander, Kuribayashi Tadamichi, abandoned beach defence and banzai charges; his men dug kilometres of tunnels and bunkers and waited.

The 4th and 5th Marine Divisions landed on 19 February 1945 into soft ash that bogged down vehicles, and then into fire from hidden positions across the whole island. On 23 February Marines raised the flag on Mount Suribachi; a photograph of the second, larger flag-raising became the most famous image of the Pacific war. The 3rd Division joined the battle in the centre, and the Marines fought through the northern plateau, cave by cave, with flamethrowers and demolitions.

Organised resistance ended on 26 March. Almost the entire garrison died; only some 200 were captured. By the war's end some 2,000 B-29s had made emergency landings on the island.
significance: The only major Pacific battle in which American casualties exceeded Japanese, Iwo Jima foreshadowed the cost of invading Japan itself.
uncertaintyNote: The value of the island to the bombing campaign, and whether it justified its cost, has been debated.
sources: Richard B. Frank, Downfall: The End of the Imperial Japanese Empire (1999)
Ronald H. Spector, Eagle Against the Sun (1985)
Max Hastings, Nemesis (2007)

title: Operation Spring Awakening: Lake Balaton
place: Between Lake Balaton and the Danube, western Hungary

strength.focus: 6th SS Panzer Army, 6th Army and 2nd Panzer Army, with c. 10 panzer divisions and some 800–900 tanks and assault guns
strength.opponent: 3rd Ukrainian Front, with a Bulgarian army on its southern flank

casualties: Soviet c. 33,000 killed and wounded; German losses uncertain but heavy, including several hundred armoured vehicles
summary: Hitler's last major offensive of the war, launched by the panzer army withdrawn from the Ardennes, bogs down in mud and Soviet defences in Hungary within ten days.
detail:
With Budapest lost and the Red Army on the Oder, Hitler sent Sepp Dietrich's 6th SS Panzer Army not to defend Berlin but to Hungary, to protect the last oilfields at Nagykanizsa and throw the Soviets back across the Danube. Spring Awakening opened on 6 March 1945 with attacks from both sides of Lake Balaton and from Yugoslavia in the south.

The thaw had turned the ground to mud; tanks sank to their turrets, and the Soviets, forewarned, had prepared deep belts of anti-tank defences on the Kursk pattern. The SS panzer divisions gained some 30 kilometres before the attack stalled. On 16 March Tolbukhin launched the Vienna offensive, and within days the German armies were in full retreat towards Austria. Hitler, enraged, ordered the SS divisions, including his own Leibstandarte, to remove their honorific armbands.
significance: The failure of Spring Awakening squandered Germany's last armoured reserve, opened the road to Vienna, and ended any German offensive capacity in the war.
uncertaintyNote: German strength and loss figures differ widely between sources; the Soviet figure is Krivosheev's for the Balaton defensive operation.
sources: David M. Glantz and Jonathan House, When Titans Clashed (rev. ed. 2015)
Earl F. Ziemke, Stalingrad to Berlin: The German Defeat in the East (1968)
Ian Kershaw, The End: Hitler's Germany 1944–45 (2011)

title: Remagen and the Rhine crossings
place: The Ludendorff railway bridge at Remagen, and the Rhine from Wesel to Oppenheim
summary: American troops find the railway bridge at Remagen still standing and rush across the Rhine. Within three weeks Patton and Montgomery have crossed in force, and the last barrier into Germany is gone.
detail:
On 7 March 1945 a task force of the US 9th Armored Division reached the heights above Remagen and saw the Ludendorff railway bridge intact. As American infantry ran onto it, the German defenders fired their demolition charges, but the bridge lifted and settled back. Within a day thousands of troops were across. Hitler had several officers court-martialled and shot, and replaced Rundstedt with Kesselring as commander in the west. The damaged bridge collapsed on 17 March, but pontoon bridges were already in place.

On the night of 22–23 March Patton's Third Army crossed almost unopposed at Oppenheim. On 23–24 March Montgomery's 21st Army Group crossed near Wesel after an enormous bombardment, supported by Operation Varsity, the largest airborne drop of the war in a single day.

The Allied armies then encircled the Ruhr, trapping Model's Army Group B; more than 300,000 men surrendered in April, and Model shot himself.
significance: The crossing of the Rhine removed Germany's last great natural defence in the west and opened the way into the heart of the Reich.
uncertaintyNote: Accounts differ on why the Remagen charges failed: faulty fuses, a hit on the main circuit, or a weak commercial explosive.
sources: Rick Atkinson, The Guns at Last Light (2013)
Charles B. MacDonald, The Last Offensive (US Army official history, 1973)
Max Hastings, Armageddon: The Battle for Germany 1944–45 (2004)

title: Firebombing of Tokyo
place: Tokyo, chiefly the districts east of the Sumida river
casualties: c. 80,000–100,000 killed; c. 1 million made homeless
summary: Some 300 B-29s fly low over Tokyo at night with incendiary bombs. The fire destroys about 40 square kilometres of the city and kills perhaps 100,000 people, the deadliest air raid in history.
detail:
High-altitude precision bombing of Japanese factories had achieved little, and Curtis LeMay, commanding the B-29s in the Marianas, changed tactics. Stripping his bombers of most guns to carry more bombs, he sent them in at low altitude, at night, against the most densely built districts of Tokyo, where small workshops fed Japanese industry among wooden homes.

In the night of 9–10 March 1945 some 330 B-29s took off, and the leading aircraft marked the target with fire. The napalm-filled bombs that followed, driven by a strong wind, raised a conflagration that engulfed the working-class districts east of the Sumida. People sheltering in canals and the river were boiled or drowned; others died in the streets as the fire outran them. About 40 square kilometres burned.

Over the following months the same methods were turned on Nagoya, Osaka, Kobe and almost every Japanese city of any size, killing several hundred thousand more civilians before the atomic bombs.
significance: The Tokyo raid killed more people than any other single air attack, including Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and opened a campaign that burned out Japan's cities.
uncertaintyNote: This is an American raid on a Japanese city: following the atlas convention the city's side is 'focus' and the outcome is 'n/a'. Japanese police counted c. 83,000 dead; other estimates reach 100,000 or more.
sources: Richard B. Frank, Downfall: The End of the Imperial Japanese Empire (1999)
Max Hastings, Nemesis (2007)
Ronald H. Spector, Eagle Against the Sun (1985)

title: Battle of Okinawa
place: Okinawa, Ryukyu Islands, and the seas around it
casualties: Japanese c. 75,000–110,000 soldiers; Okinawan civilians c. 100,000–150,000; US c. 12,500 dead (including c. 4,900 at sea) and c. 36,000 wounded
summary: The last and bloodiest battle of the Pacific war. For 82 days Americans fight across Okinawa while kamikazes strike the fleet; the giant battleship Yamato is sunk on a one-way sortie, and civilians die in vast numbers.
detail:
On 1 April 1945 four American divisions landed unopposed on Okinawa's Hagushi beaches. Ushijima's Thirty-Second Army waited in the south, dug into ridges around Shuri Castle, and there the battle became an attritional struggle through the spring rains, ridge by ridge.
