At sea, Japan launched waves of kamikaze aircraft against the fleet, sinking some 30 ships and damaging hundreds; the US Navy suffered its heaviest losses of the war. On 6 April the battleship Yamato sailed on a one-way mission with fuel to reach Okinawa and beach herself as a fortress; on 7 April, south-west of Kyushu, American carrier aircraft sank her with some 3,000 of her crew.

The Shuri line was abandoned at the end of May, and the remnants retreated to the southern tip, where they were crowded together with civilians. Buckner was killed on 18 June; Ushijima took his life around 22 June. Okinawan civilians, a quarter or more of the population, died in crossfire, of hunger, at the hands of Japanese soldiers, and in suicides that the army urged or forced upon them.
significance: Okinawa's toll shaped American estimates of the cost of invading Japan, and so the decision to use the atomic bomb; the island remained under US rule until 1972.
uncertaintyNote: Japanese military and civilian death figures overlap, because many Okinawans were conscripted, and estimates vary widely. The point is central Okinawa; a marker shows where Yamato sank.
sources: George Feifer, Tennozan: The Battle of Okinawa and the Atomic Bomb (1992)
Richard B. Frank, Downfall: The End of the Imperial Japanese Empire (1999)
Max Hastings, Nemesis (2007)

title: Liberation of Bergen-Belsen and Dachau
place: Bergen-Belsen, near Celle, Lower Saxony; Buchenwald near Weimar; Dachau near Munich

sides.opponent: Camp prisoners; British and US forces

casualties: At Bergen-Belsen c. 10,000 unburied dead were found and c. 13,000 more died after liberation; tens of thousands died in the camps of the Reich in the last months of the war
summary: American and British troops reach the concentration camps inside Germany: Buchenwald on 11 April, Bergen-Belsen on 15 April, Dachau on 29 April. What they find, filmed and broadcast, shocks the world.
detail:
In the war's last months the camps inside Germany filled with prisoners driven west on death marches from the east. Food and sanitation collapsed; typhus and starvation killed tens of thousands. At Bergen-Belsen, where Anne and Margot Frank had died in February or March, the death rate soared.

On 11 April 1945 American troops reached Buchenwald, near Weimar, where prisoners had taken control as the SS fled. On 15 April, under a local truce, the British 11th Armoured Division entered Bergen-Belsen and found some 60,000 prisoners, many dying, and around 10,000 unburied bodies. Despite medical relief, some 13,000 more died in the following weeks. On 29 April the US Seventh Army reached Dachau, the first concentration camp, opened in 1933, and found a train of wagons filled with corpses; some SS guards were killed by enraged soldiers.

The Allied commanders made German civilians and soldiers visit the camps, and press photographs, newsreels and the BBC's broadcasts from Belsen carried the scenes across the world.
significance: The liberation of the western camps fixed the image of Nazi crimes in Western memory and provided much of the evidence later heard at Nuremberg.
uncertaintyNote: The atlas treats the camps as sites of atrocity, so 'n/a'. Belsen was not an extermination camp of the Birkenau type, though mass death there was the result of deliberate neglect; numbers of dead are approximate.
sources: Nikolaus Wachsmann, KL: A History of the Nazi Concentration Camps (2015)
Ben Shephard, After Daybreak: The Liberation of Belsen, 1945 (2005)
Dan Stone, The Liberation of the Camps (2015)

title: Battle of Berlin and Hitler's suicide
place: Berlin and the Oder–Neisse front

strength.focus: c. 750,000–1,000,000 on the Oder–Neisse front, including Volkssturm and Hitler Youth

casualties: Soviet and Polish c. 360,000, including c. 80,000 killed; German c. 90,000–100,000 dead and some 480,000 captured; tens of thousands of civilians
summary: Zhukov and Konev storm across the Oder and Neisse and encircle Berlin. As Soviet troops fight towards the Reichstag, Hitler kills himself in his bunker on 30 April; the city surrenders on 2 May.
detail:
On 16 April 1945 Zhukov's 1st Belorussian Front attacked the Seelow Heights above the Oder, where Heinrici's defenders held him for three costly days; Konev's 1st Ukrainian Front broke across the Neisse further south, and Stalin let the two marshals race for the capital. By 25 April Berlin was encircled, and the same day Soviet and American troops met on the Elbe.

The city was defended by remnants of army units, Waffen-SS, including foreign volunteers, old men of the Volkssturm and boys of the Hitler Youth. Soviet armies fought inward street by street under massive artillery fire, while civilians sheltered in cellars and U-Bahn tunnels. In the bunker beneath the Reich Chancellery Hitler married Eva Braun on 29 April; on the afternoon of 30 April, with Soviet troops a few hundred metres away, both took their own lives. Goebbels and his wife killed their six children and themselves the next day.

The Reichstag was stormed on 30 April–1 May, and on 2 May General Weidling surrendered the city. Soviet soldiers raped very large numbers of Berlin's women in the weeks that followed.
significance: The fall of Berlin and the death of Hitler ended the Third Reich; Germany's surrender followed within a week.
uncertaintyNote: German military and civilian losses in Berlin are poorly documented and estimates vary widely; Soviet losses are Krivosheev's figures for the whole operation.
sources: Antony Beevor, Berlin: The Downfall 1945 (2002)
Ian Kershaw, Hitler 1936–1945: Nemesis (2000)
Ian Kershaw, The End: Germany 1944–45 (2011)
David M. Glantz and Jonathan M. House, When Titans Clashed (1995)

title: Meeting on the Elbe
place: Torgau and Strehla, on the Elbe, Saxony
summary: Patrols of the US 69th Infantry Division meet Soviet soldiers on the Elbe at Strehla and Torgau. The armies from east and west have joined, and Germany is cut in two.
detail:
In April 1945 the American armies, having crossed Germany from the Rhine, halted on the Elbe and the Mulde by Eisenhower's decision, leaving Berlin to the Red Army. Patrols probed eastward to find the Soviets advancing from the Oder.

On 25 April a patrol under Lieutenant Albert Kotzebue crossed the Elbe near Strehla and met soldiers of the Soviet 58th Guards Rifle Division. Later the same day Lieutenant William Robertson's patrol met Soviet troops on the wrecked bridge at Torgau. Official ceremonies, photographs and toasts followed, and 25 April became 'Elbe Day'. In Moscow, Washington and London the news was announced simultaneously.

The riverbanks were also crowded with German refugees and soldiers trying to cross westward to surrender to the Americans rather than the Soviets.
significance: The link-up split the remains of the Reich into a northern and a southern half, and the handshake on the Elbe became a symbol of wartime alliance soon overtaken by the Cold War.
uncertaintyNote: There was no battle here, so the outcome is 'n/a'. The first contact was at Strehla, a few hours before the more famous meeting at Torgau.
sources: Antony Beevor, Berlin: The Downfall 1945 (2002)
Rick Atkinson, The Guns at Last Light (2013)
Charles B. MacDonald, The Last Offensive (US Army official history, 1973)

title: Death of Mussolini
place: Giulino di Mezzegra, Lake Como, Italy
summary: Fleeing towards Switzerland with a German column, Mussolini is caught by partisans at Dongo. The next day he and Clara Petacci are shot; their bodies are hung in a Milan square.
detail:
Since his rescue by German commandos in 1943 Mussolini had headed the Italian Social Republic, a puppet state at Salò under German control, while Italy endured civil war as well as foreign occupation. In April 1945 the Allied spring offensive broke through into the Po valley and partisans rose in the northern cities.

Mussolini left Milan on 25 April. On 27 April, at Dongo on Lake Como, partisans of the 52nd Garibaldi Brigade stopped the German column he had joined and found him in a German greatcoat. On 28 April he and his mistress, Clara Petacci, were shot at Giulino di Mezzegra, by the account later made official at the hands of Walter Audisio, sent by the communist-led resistance command; other fascist leaders were shot at Dongo.

On 29 April the bodies were hung upside down from the roof of a petrol station in Piazzale Loreto in Milan, where fascists had displayed the bodies of fifteen executed partisans the previous August. That day German representatives signed the surrender of their forces in Italy at Caserta, effective on 2 May.
significance: Mussolini's death ended Italian Fascism, two days before Hitler's suicide, and the scenes at Piazzale Loreto remain a contested image in Italy's memory of the war.
uncertaintyNote: The details of the execution, including who fired the shots and the exact time and place, have been disputed by Italian historians and journalists for decades.
sources: R.J.B. Bosworth, Mussolini (2002)
Denis Mack Smith, Mussolini (1981)
Sergio Luzzatto, The Body of Il Duce (1998; Eng. trans. 2005)

title: Rangoon retaken
place: Rangoon (Yangon), Burma (Myanmar)
summary: Racing the monsoon down from Meiktila, Slim's army nears Rangoon as a seaborne force lands at the river mouth. The Japanese have already gone; the capital of Burma is retaken without a fight.
detail:
After Imphal, Slim's Fourteenth Army crossed the Chindwin and the Irrawaddy. In March 1945 a bold thrust took Meiktila, the Japanese base in central Burma, and Mandalay fell; the Burma Area Army under Kimura was broken. Aung San's Burma National Army, armed by Japan, turned against its sponsors at the end of March.

Slim's columns then drove south down the road and railway towards Rangoon, racing to reach the port before the monsoon cut supplies. To make sure of it, Operation Dracula was launched from the sea: on 1 May Gurkha paratroops landed at Elephant Point to clear the river mouth, and on 2 May the 26th Indian Division came ashore. Kimura had already evacuated the city. An RAF pilot flying over the jail saw that Allied prisoners had painted on its roof that the Japanese had gone. The troops entered on 3 May.

The Fourteenth Army's spearheads, held up by fighting and the first rains around Pegu, linked up a few days later.
significance: The recapture of Rangoon completed the reconquest of most of Burma, the longest British land campaign of the war, though Japanese forces fought on in the hills until August.
uncertaintyNote: The exact wording painted on the jail roof is reported differently in different accounts.
sources: William Slim, Defeat into Victory (1956)
Christopher Bayly and Tim Harper, Forgotten Armies (2004)
Louis Allen, Burma: The Longest War 1941–45 (1984)

title: Prague Uprising
place: Prague
casualties: Czech insurgents and civilians c. 1,700 killed; German c. 1,000; Soviet c. 30 in the city itself; figures approximate
summary: As the Reich collapses, the people of Prague rise against the German garrison and throw up barricades. After four days of fighting the Germans capitulate, and the Red Army enters on 9 May.
detail:
On the morning of 5 May 1945 Czech insurgents seized the radio building in Prague and broadcast an appeal to the city to rise. Some 1,600 barricades went up, and police, former soldiers and civilians fought German troops and SS units for control of the city, while the Waffen-SS used armour and committed reprisal killings.

The insurgents received unexpected help from the 1st Division of the Russian Liberation Army, Soviet prisoners who had joined the Germans under General Vlasov and now changed sides, hoping to win Western protection; they withdrew on 7 May. The American Third Army, only some 80 km away at Pilsen, was held back by agreement with the Soviets.

On 8 May the German commander, General Rudolf Toussaint, signed a capitulation allowing his troops to leave westward. Konev's tank armies, racing from Berlin and Dresden, entered Prague on 9 May and destroyed the last German forces of Army Group Centre in Bohemia over the following days. Violence against Prague's German civilians followed the liberation.
significance: The Prague rising was the last major battle of the war in Europe, and its liberation by the Red Army shaped Czechoslovakia's post-war turn to the east.
uncertaintyNote: Casualty figures vary. The event begins before VE Day and so belongs to the 'collapse' chapter.
sources: Chad Bryant, Prague in Black: Nazi Rule and Czech Nationalism (2007)
Antony Beevor, Berlin: The Downfall 1945 (2002)
Ian Kershaw, The End: Germany 1944–45 (2011)

title: Germany surrenders: VE Day
place: Berlin-Karlshorst, after the signing at Reims

sides.opponent: United States, Britain, the Soviet Union and France

summary: Germany's armed forces surrender unconditionally, signed at Reims early on 7 May and again in Berlin late on 8 May. Crowds fill the streets of the Allied capitals: the war in Europe is over.
detail:
After Hitler's death, Grand Admiral Dönitz, his designated successor, tried to surrender to the Western Allies piecemeal while letting soldiers and civilians escape the Red Army. German forces in Italy had surrendered on 2 May; on 4 May Montgomery accepted the surrender of those in north-west Germany, the Netherlands and Denmark on Lüneburg Heath.

Eisenhower insisted on unconditional surrender on all fronts. At 2.41 a.m. on 7 May, in a schoolhouse at Reims that served as his headquarters, General Alfred Jodl signed the act of surrender, to take effect at 23.01 Central European Time on 8 May. Stalin demanded a second ceremony in Berlin, before Soviet commanders. Late on 8 May at Karlshorst, Field Marshal Keitel signed again in the presence of Zhukov, Tedder and American and French representatives; in Moscow it was already 9 May, which became the Soviet Union's Victory Day.

Crowds celebrated in London, Paris, New York and Moscow. In Germany fighting flickered on in places, and the Dönitz government was arrested at Flensburg on 23 May.
significance: The surrender ended almost six years of war in Europe, in which tens of millions had died, and left Germany wholly occupied and without a government of its own.
uncertaintyNote: The event is dated to 8 May, the day of the Berlin signing and of VE Day; the first signing at Reims was in the early hours of 7 May. Soviet and successor states mark 9 May.
sources: Ian Kershaw, The End: Germany 1944–45 (2011)
Antony Beevor, Berlin: The Downfall 1945 (2002)
Gerhard L. Weinberg, A World at Arms (1994)

title: Landing at Balikpapan
place: Balikpapan, south-east Borneo (Indonesia)

strength.opponent: 7th Australian Division and supporting forces, c. 33,000 men

casualties: Australian 229 killed and 634 wounded; Japanese over 2,000 killed and 63 captured
summary: The Australian 7th Division storms the oil port of Balikpapan in Borneo, in the last large amphibious landing of the war.
detail:
The Borneo campaign of 1945, Operation Oboe, was meant to recover the island's oilfields and give the Allies bases for a move on Java. After landings at Tarakan in May and at Brunei Bay in June, the 7th Australian Division was landed at Balikpapan on 1 July 1945, after sixteen days of air attack and minesweeping and one of the heaviest naval bombardments of the Pacific war. MacArthur came ashore to watch.

The Australians took the town and the refineries in the first days, then pushed inland against Japanese troops holding the ridges and the road to Samarinda; organised resistance ended late in July, though skirmishing went on until the surrender in August. The oil installations, wrecked by bombing and demolitions, produced nothing before the war ended.
significance: Balikpapan was the largest amphibious operation carried out by Australian forces; whether these last Borneo landings were worth their cost is still debated.
uncertaintyNote: Japanese strength and losses are estimates; the official history gives the Australian casualty figures.
sources: Gavin Long, The Final Campaigns (Australian official history, 1963)
Max Hastings, Nemesis: The Battle for Japan, 1944–45 (2007)
Peter Dennis et al., The Oxford Companion to Australian Military History (2nd ed. 2008)

title: Potsdam Conference
place: Cecilienhof Palace, Potsdam

sides.focus: Japan and occupied Germany (the subjects of the conference)
sides.opponent: United States, Britain and the Soviet Union

summary: Truman, Stalin and Churchill, replaced midway by Attlee, settle the occupation of Germany and Poland's new western border. The Potsdam Declaration calls on Japan to surrender or face 'prompt and utter destruction'.
detail:
The last wartime conference of the Big Three met in the Cecilienhof palace from 17 July 1945. Truman had succeeded Roosevelt in April; Churchill left in the middle to hear the results of the British general election and was replaced by the new Labour prime minister, Clement Attlee.

The Allies agreed to govern Germany through a Control Council, with four occupation zones; it was to be disarmed, denazified and democratised, and reparations were to be taken largely from each power's own zone. The lands east of the Oder and Neisse were placed under Polish administration pending a peace treaty, and the conference approved the 'orderly and humane' transfer of German populations from Poland, Czechoslovakia and Hungary. In practice the expulsions, which displaced some 12 million Germans, were often brutal.

On 16 July the first atomic bomb had been tested in New Mexico, and on 24 July Truman told Stalin that the United States had a new weapon of unusual destructive force. On 26 July the United States, Britain and China issued the Potsdam Declaration, demanding Japan's unconditional surrender. Japan's government did not accept it.
significance: Potsdam drew the lines of post-war Germany and Poland and delivered the ultimatum that preceded the atomic bombings; the strains between the Allies were already plain.
uncertaintyNote: This was a conference, so the outcome is 'n/a'; the 'focus' slot names the Axis states whose fate it decided. The Japanese prime minister's response to the Declaration, often translated as 'ignore it', is debated.
sources: Michael Neiberg, Potsdam: The End of World War II and the Remaking of Europe (2015)
Tsuyoshi Hasegawa, Racing the Enemy (2005)
R.M. Douglas, Orderly and Humane: The Expulsion of the Germans after the Second World War (2012)

title: Sinking of USS Indianapolis
place: Philippine Sea, between Guam and Leyte

strength.opponent: Heavy cruiser Indianapolis, sailing unescorted with 1,195 men

casualties: 879 of 1,195 men died, c. 300 in the sinking and the rest of exposure, thirst and shark attacks over four days in the water; 316 survived
summary: Days after delivering the parts of the Hiroshima atomic bomb to Tinian, the cruiser Indianapolis is torpedoed and sunk; most of her crew die in the sea before they are found.
detail:
Indianapolis carried the uranium core and components of the Little Boy bomb from San Francisco to Tinian, arriving on 26 July 1945. She then sailed alone for Leyte. Shortly after midnight on 30 July the Japanese submarine I-58 hit her with two torpedoes; she sank in about twelve minutes, too fast for a proper distress call to be acknowledged.

Around 900 men went into the water, many without lifeboats. No one ashore noticed that the ship had failed to arrive, and for four days the survivors drifted, dying of wounds, exposure, saltwater poisoning and repeated shark attacks. A patrol plane spotted them by chance on 2 August; 316 were rescued.

Captain McVay was court-martialled for failing to zigzag, the only US captain so tried among the hundreds who lost ships in the war. Hashimoto testified that zigzagging would have made no difference. McVay was formally exonerated by Congress in 2000.
significance: The worst single loss at sea in US naval history, the sinking was the last major US warship lost to enemy action in the war and exposed failures in the navy's tracking of its own ships.
sources: Lynn Vincent and Sara Vladic, Indianapolis: The True Story of the Worst Sea Disaster in US Naval History (2018)
Richard F. Newcomb, Abandon Ship! (1958)
Samuel Eliot Morison, History of United States Naval Operations in World War II, vol. XIV (1960)

title: Atomic bombing of Hiroshima
place: Hiroshima, Honshu, Japan
casualties: c. 70,000–80,000 killed outright; c. 140,000 dead by the end of 1945, including many Korean labourers
summary: A single American bomb, a uranium weapon called Little Boy, destroys Hiroshima. Tens of thousands die in an instant, and by the end of the year perhaps 140,000 are dead of burns, injuries and radiation.
detail:
At 8.15 on the morning of 6 August 1945 the B-29 Enola Gay, flown by Colonel Paul Tibbets from Tinian, dropped Little Boy over the centre of Hiroshima, a city of some 300,000 people and the headquarters of the army defending southern Japan. The bomb exploded about 600 metres above the ground near the Aioi Bridge.

The flash and heat burned people in the open several kilometres away; the blast flattened most buildings within about two kilometres, and fires consumed what remained. Many of the dead were schoolchildren mobilised to clear firebreaks. Thousands of Korean forced labourers and some American prisoners of war were among the victims. Survivors, the hibakusha, suffered in the following weeks and years from radiation sickness, cancers and lasting injury.

Truman announced that the bomb harnessed the basic power of the universe, and warned Japan of a 'rain of ruin'. Japan's leaders, still hoping for Soviet mediation, did not at once agree to surrender.
significance: The first use of a nuclear weapon in war opened the atomic age; the decision and its role in Japan's surrender are still argued over.
uncertaintyNote: This is an American attack on a Japanese city: following the atlas convention the city's side is 'focus' and the outcome is 'n/a'. Death tolls are estimates; the city's figure of c. 140,000 by December 1945 is widely used.
sources: Richard Rhodes, The Making of the Atomic Bomb (1986)
Richard B. Frank, Downfall: The End of the Imperial Japanese Empire (1999)
Tsuyoshi Hasegawa, Racing the Enemy (2005)
John Hersey, Hiroshima (1946)

title: Soviet invasion of Manchuria
place: Manchuria (Manchukuo), northern Korea, southern Sakhalin and the Kurils
casualties: Soviet c. 12,000 killed; Japanese c. 80,000 or more killed and c. 600,000 taken prisoner; very heavy losses among Japanese settlers
summary: Just after midnight on 9 August, three Soviet fronts invade Manchuria from west, north and east. The hollowed-out Kwantung Army collapses within days, and Japan's last hope of Soviet mediation dies.
detail:
As promised at Yalta, the Soviet Union declared war on Japan on 8 August 1945, three months after Germany's surrender, and attacked in the first hour of 9 August. Vasilevsky commanded some 1.5 million troops, many of them veterans moved across Siberia since the spring. Malinovsky's Transbaikal Front crossed the Greater Khingan mountains and the desert from Mongolia; Meretskov's 1st Far Eastern Front broke in from the Maritime Province, and Purkayev's 2nd Far Eastern Front crossed the Amur.

The Kwantung Army, once Japan's finest, had been stripped of men and equipment for the Pacific. Its fortified zones were bypassed or overrun, and Soviet tank armies drove deep into the Manchurian plain within a week. After the emperor's broadcast of 15 August, Yamada ordered his forces to surrender; Soviet troops reached Harbin, Mukden and Port Arthur by airborne landings and kept advancing into northern Korea, southern Sakhalin and the Kurils into early September.

Japanese settlers caught in the collapse died in great numbers from violence, hunger, disease and mass suicide; some 600,000 prisoners were taken to labour camps in the Soviet Union, where many died.
significance: The Soviet entry into the war, coming with the atomic bombs, was decisive in persuading Japan's leaders to surrender, and it gave the Soviet Union a foothold in Manchuria and northern Korea that shaped post-war Asia.
uncertaintyNote: Japanese losses are poorly documented and estimates vary widely. Whether the atomic bombs or the Soviet attack weighed more in Japan's surrender is a major historiographical debate.
sources: David M. Glantz, The Soviet Strategic Offensive in Manchuria, 1945: 'August Storm' (2003)
Tsuyoshi Hasegawa, Racing the Enemy (2005)
Richard B. Frank, Downfall: The End of the Imperial Japanese Empire (1999)

title: Atomic bombing of Nagasaki
place: Nagasaki, Kyushu, Japan
casualties: c. 40,000 killed outright; c. 70,000–74,000 dead by the end of 1945
summary: Three days after Hiroshima, a plutonium bomb falls on Nagasaki. Clouds over Kokura, the first target, send the B-29 to its secondary target; some 70,000 people are dead by the year's end.
detail:
The second bomb, Fat Man, was a plutonium implosion weapon of the type tested in New Mexico. On the morning of 9 August 1945 the B-29 Bockscar, flown by Major Charles Sweeney, found its primary target, the arsenal city of Kokura, hidden by haze and smoke and, short of fuel, turned to Nagasaki.

The bomb exploded at 11.02 over the Urakami valley, some three kilometres from the intended aiming point. The hills that enclosed the valley contained the blast and spared much of the old harbour city, but the Urakami district, with the Mitsubishi arms works, schools, a prison and the cathedral at the heart of Japan's oldest Catholic community, was obliterated. Prisoners of war and Korean labourers were among the dead.

That night, with Soviet armies pouring into Manchuria and Nagasaki destroyed, Japan's Supreme War Council remained deadlocked on surrender. Shortly before dawn on 10 August, at an imperial conference, Emperor Hirohito declared that Japan should accept the Potsdam terms.
significance: Nagasaki is the last city attacked with a nuclear weapon; together with Hiroshima and the Soviet invasion it brought Japan's surrender.
uncertaintyNote: This is an American attack on a Japanese city: following the atlas convention the city's side is 'focus' and the outcome is 'n/a'. Death tolls are estimates.
sources: Richard Rhodes, The Making of the Atomic Bomb (1986)
Richard B. Frank, Downfall: The End of the Imperial Japanese Empire (1999)
Susan Southard, Nagasaki: Life After Nuclear War (2015)

title: Japan surrenders in Tokyo Bay
place: Aboard USS Missouri, Tokyo Bay
summary: On the deck of the battleship Missouri, Japan's foreign minister and army chief of staff sign the instrument of surrender before MacArthur and the Allied representatives. The Second World War is over.
detail:
After the emperor's decision of 10 August, Japan offered to accept the Potsdam Declaration provided the imperial prerogatives were preserved; the Allied reply was ambiguous. On 14 August Hirohito again broke the deadlock in favour of surrender. That night army officers tried to seize the palace and destroy the recording of his speech, but the coup failed. At noon on 15 August the Japanese people heard their emperor's voice for the first time, announcing that the war situation had developed not necessarily to Japan's advantage.

On 2 September, in Tokyo Bay, Foreign Minister Shigemitsu Mamoru and General Umezu Yoshijirō signed the instrument of surrender aboard USS Missouri. MacArthur signed as Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, followed by Nimitz and representatives of China, Britain, the Soviet Union, Australia, Canada, France, the Netherlands and New Zealand. The ceremony took little more than twenty minutes.

Japanese forces surrendered locally across Asia in the weeks that followed, at Nanjing, Singapore, Hong Kong and elsewhere, and prisoners and internees were freed from camps where many had died.
significance: The surrender ended the Second World War, in which some 70–85 million people had died, and began the American occupation of Japan.
uncertaintyNote: The Missouri's anchorage is placed approximately in Tokyo Bay off Yokosuka. Fighting with Soviet forces continued in places into early September.
sources: Richard B. Frank, Downfall: The End of the Imperial Japanese Empire (1999)
Tsuyoshi Hasegawa, Racing the Enemy (2005)
John W. Dower, Embracing Defeat (1999)
Herbert P. Bix, Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan (2000)
